0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 14–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a commission but with a question: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. <sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God. <sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. <sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men. <sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. <sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. <sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. <sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. <sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, <sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. <sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. <sup>29</sup>The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! <sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” <sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
John's prologue (vv. 1–18) is the most compressed theological statement ever written. In eighteen verses John moves from eternity (“in the beginning”) to incarnation (“the Word became flesh”) and establishes the entire theological framework for what follows. The Word (Logos) was not created — he was “in the beginning,” which is the opening phrase of Genesis. He was “with God” (distinct from the Father) and “was God” (identical in nature). He is the agent of all creation and the source of all life. And then the most astonishing sentence in Scripture: “the Word became flesh.”

The prologue closes with a summary of the Gospel's plot: he came to his own and his own did not receive him (the theme of rejection that will run through chapters 1–12), but to those who received him he gave the right to become children of God — born not of human will but of God (the theme of the new birth that Nicodemus will ask about in chapter 3). John the Baptist then appears to introduce Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world — the first interpretive title for Jesus in the Gospel and the key to understanding the cross at its end. The first disciples are called, and Nathanael's confession sets the pattern: the Gospel is written to lead readers to say with him, “You are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Three prepositional phrases in one sentence establish the eternal pre-existence, the personal distinction, and the essential deity of the Son. “In the beginning” echoes Genesis 1:1 — but where Genesis begins with creation, John begins before creation, with the Word who was already there. “With God” (pros ton Theon — literally “toward God”) implies face-to-face personal relationship within the Godhead. “Was God” (Theos ēn ho Logos) — without the article before Theos, this is a predicate of nature: the Word shares the divine nature. The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) would reach for this verse as the foundation of Trinitarian orthodoxy: the Son is homoousios — of the same substance as the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.”
verseByVerse.commentary: “Became flesh” (sarx egeneto) is the most radical statement in John's prologue. The eternal Son did not merely appear in human form; he assumed a full human nature — body, soul, emotions, limitations — without surrendering his divine nature. “Dwelt” (eskēnōsen — literally “pitched his tent” or “tabernacled”) evokes the wilderness tabernacle where God's glory dwelt among Israel (Exod 40:34–35). The glory that once filled the tent is now present in a human body. “We have seen his glory” — John claims eyewitness testimony (cf. 1 John 1:1–3). The signs throughout the Gospel are what John means: the glory of the Father shining through the Son's flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: “To all who did receive him… he gave the right to become children of God.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gospel's soteriological logic is compressed here: receiving Christ (faith) produces the right to be called God's children. Verse 13 immediately defines the origin of this new birth: not of blood (Jewish ancestry), not of the will of the flesh (human decision in its natural state), not of the will of man (another person's choice for you), but of God. This is the Johannine equivalent of Paul's “by grace through faith, not of yourselves.” The new birth is a divine act; the receiving is a human act; both are real. John holds both without resolving the tension, because both are true.

verseByVerse.quote: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the interpretive key to the entire Gospel. Before Jesus has done a single sign or said a single word in John, he is identified as the Lamb of God. The background is layered: the Passover lamb (Exod 12), whose blood protected from the angel of death; the daily temple sacrifice; and above all the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, who is “led like a lamb to the slaughter” and who “bore the sin of many.” John places the Baptist's cry at the beginning so the reader watches every subsequent chapter knowing where it is heading. The crucifixion in John 19 happens on the day of Passover preparation, at the hour when the lambs were being slaughtered. The Lamb of God dies as the true Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' word to Nathanael alludes to Jacob's ladder (Gen 28:12) — the stairway between heaven and earth on which angels moved. Jesus declares himself to be that stairway: the meeting point of heaven and earth, the one in whom the divine and the human are permanently joined. This is the first use of “Son of Man” in John — the Daniel 7:13 figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. John's Gospel will use “Son of Man” consistently for Jesus in his role as the one who descends from heaven and ascends back to the Father (3:13; 6:62). The ladder has become a person.

1.theology: The eternal Sonship and the incarnation. John 1 is the New Testament's most direct statement of the pre-existence and deity of the Son. Against every Christological heresy — Arianism (the Son is a created being), Docetism (the Son only appeared to be human), Adoptionism (the Son became divine at his baptism) — John asserts: he was God from eternity, he became genuinely human at the incarnation, and he remains both forever. The technical term is the hypostatic union: two natures (divine and human), one person (the eternal Son). This is not a philosophical puzzle but a pastoral necessity: only the one who is fully God can reveal the Father; only the one who is fully human can represent us before the Father. The Lamb of God must be both to take away the sin of the world.
1.examples:
Then: John's prologue was written into a world saturated with Greek philosophy (Logos was a central concept in Stoicism — the rational principle governing the universe) and Jewish wisdom theology. John takes the Logos concept and fills it with a person: the Word is not an impersonal rational principle but the personal, relational, incarnate Son of God. He answers the Greek quest for ultimate rationality and the Jewish quest for divine wisdom with the same answer: Jesus.

Now: Every generation asks the question Nathanael asked: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (v. 46). The answer is the same: “Come and see.” The Gospel of John is itself the answer — a sustained presentation of who Jesus is, written for people on the edge of faith. The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world is still taking away sin. The invitation to come and see is still open.

2.title: The New Temple and the New Birth
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. <sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples. <sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim. <sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom <sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.” <sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. <sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade.” <sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” <sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 contains two scenes that together announce the theme of replacement and fulfilment: the old order giving way to the new. At Cana, water stored in Jewish purification jars is transformed into the finest wine — the old rites of purification are superseded by the wine of the messianic banquet. At Jerusalem, the temple courts are cleansed, and Jesus announces that he himself is the true temple: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” In John's Gospel this cleansing comes at the beginning of the ministry rather than the end (as in the Synoptics), functioning as a programmatic statement of what Jesus' entire ministry means.

The two scenes interpret each other. The wine is the new, abundant, joyful life of the messianic age; the temple is the place where God dwells with his people and where sacrifice is made. Jesus is both: the source of the new wine and the true temple. In him, the presence of God and the means of atonement are not located in a building in Jerusalem but in a person who can be encountered anywhere in the world. John tells us the disciples remembered this word after the resurrection and believed — faith here, as throughout John, is the appropriate response to the revelation of who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: “You have kept the good wine until now.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The master of the feast's words are an unwitting prophecy. The old covenant order — represented by the six stone jars for Jewish purification — has given way to something better. In the Old Testament, wine is a sign of the messianic age: “the mountains shall drip sweet wine” (Amos 9:13). Jesus' first sign is a statement in water and wine: the age of fulfilment has arrived. The best wine was kept for last, as Paul will say: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Gal 4:4). Six jars — one short of seven, the number of perfection — suggest incompleteness; the true completion is now present.

verseByVerse.quote: “This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory.”
verseByVerse.commentary: John calls the miracles “signs” (sēmeia), not “wonders” or “works of power” — because signs point beyond themselves to something else. Each sign in John is a window into the identity of Jesus, and they are arranged to build toward the climactic seventh sign (the raising of Lazarus) and the eighth (the resurrection). The disciples “believed in him” — this is the intended response to every sign. The signs are not ends in themselves; they are invitations to faith in the one who performs them.

verseByVerse.quote: “Do not make my Father's house a house of trade.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus calls the temple “my Father's house” — a statement of divine Sonship that his opponents will understand perfectly. The temple was meant to be the place where all nations could pray (Isa 56:7); the Court of the Gentiles had been turned into a market. Jesus' cleansing is both prophetic judgment (Mal 3:1–3 anticipated the Lord's sudden coming to his temple to purify it) and a claim of authority over the house of his Father. The zeal that “consumes” him (Ps 69:9, quoted in v. 17) is not mere anger but the burning concern of the Son for the honour of the Father's dwelling.

verseByVerse.quote: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This saying is the most important theological statement in chapter 2. The physical temple in Jerusalem will be destroyed (fulfilled in AD 70); Jesus' body will be destroyed and raised in three days. The two temples — stone and flesh — are parallel: both are the dwelling place of God, both are destroyed, and the resurrection of the true temple makes the stone temple permanently redundant. From the resurrection onward, wherever Jesus is present through his Spirit, there is the temple. The church is his body (Eph 1:23); individual believers are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19). The entire sacrificial and liturgical system of Israel has been absorbed into his person.

verseByVerse.quote: “But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Many believed in Jesus because of his signs, but Jesus did not “believe in” them in return. He knew what was in them. The same divine knowledge that will expose the Samaritan woman's past (4:18) and Judas' betrayal (6:70–71) is at work here. Sign-faith is not necessarily saving faith; it is possible to be impressed by Jesus without being truly surrendered to him. John's Gospel will repeatedly distinguish superficial enthusiasm from genuine, persevering faith — the faith that holds on through the cross.

2.theology: Christ as the true temple. The temple theology of John 2 is one of the most important strands in New Testament biblical theology. The Jerusalem temple was the centrepiece of Israel's covenant life: the place of God's dwelling, the site of sacrifice, the location of prayer, the goal of pilgrimage. Jesus replaces all of this — not by abolishing it but by being its fulfilment and its antitype. He is the true dwelling of God (1:14 — “tabernacled among us”); he is the true sacrifice (1:29 — the Lamb of God); he is the true meeting place of heaven and earth (1:51). After the resurrection, the temple in Jerusalem becomes theologically redundant, which is why its physical destruction in AD 70 is not a catastrophe for the people of God — their true temple has been raised and is alive forever.
2.examples:
Then: The disciples did not fully understand the word about the temple until after the resurrection (v. 22). This is a pattern in John's Gospel: the disciples receive words they cannot yet understand, and the Spirit brings them to remembrance and illumination after the cross. The Christian reads the whole Gospel in the light of the resurrection — and everything looks different from that vantage point.

Now: The replacement of external religion with the living presence of Christ is the permanent revolution of the Gospel. We do not need a temple, a priest, or a sacrifice — we have Christ, who is all three. Every time the church gathers at the Lord's Supper, we are at the true temple, offered the true sacrifice, in the presence of the true priest who has passed through the heavenly curtain.

3.title: God So Loved the World
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.” <sup>3</sup>Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” <sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. <sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. <sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' <sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” <sup>14</sup>And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, <sup>15</sup>that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. <sup>16</sup>For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. <sup>17</sup>For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him. <sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological centre of the entire New Testament. The conversation with Nicodemus (vv. 1–21) introduces three of John's most important themes: the new birth, the lifting up of the Son of Man, and eternal life. Nicodemus comes by night — a detail John will recall at the burial of Jesus (19:39), when Nicodemus emerges from the dark into the daylight of the resurrection. He represents the best of old-covenant religion: learned, sincere, genuinely seeking. But Jesus tells him that learning and sincerity are insufficient; what is needed is a second birth, from above, by the Spirit.

The conversation opens onto the great missionary and soteriological statement at the heart of the Gospel (vv. 16–21). “God so loved the world” — not merely Israel but the whole created order. The love is measured by the gift: the only Son. The gift is measured by the condition of those who receive it: those who were perishing. The outcome is either eternal life (for those who believe) or condemnation (for those who prefer darkness). John 3:16 is not a sentimental saying about divine benevolence; it is a statement of costly, specific, saving love that demands a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: “Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The word “again” (anōthen) means both “again” and “from above” — John intends both meanings simultaneously. The new birth is a second birth and a birth from heaven. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, takes it literally (v. 4) and misses the point. Jesus clarifies: the new birth is of water and Spirit — almost certainly a reference to Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people and put a new spirit within them. This is the new covenant promise, and Jesus is announcing its arrival. The wind analogy (v. 8) is devastating in its honesty: the Spirit blows where he wills. We cannot generate the new birth, predict it, or control it. We can only receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the first of John's three “lifting up” sayings (also 8:28 and 12:32–34). Each time Jesus refers to the cross using the language of exaltation — “lifted up” in John means both crucified and glorified simultaneously. The allusion is to Numbers 21:4–9: Israelites bitten by serpents were healed by looking at the bronze serpent lifted on a pole. Jesus identifies himself as the antitype: those “bitten” by sin who look to him in faith will be healed — will have eternal life. The cross is not the defeat of the Son but his exaltation; not the destruction of God's plan but its fulfilment. John's passion narrative will develop this paradox to the full: the crucifixion is the coronation.

verseByVerse.quote: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse contains the whole gospel in one sentence, and every word carries weight. “God” — the initiative is divine; love is not our reaching up but God's reaching down. “So loved” — the “so” (houtōs) modifies manner as much as degree: this is how God loved, by giving. “The world” — not merely Israel, not merely the elect in abstraction, but the entire fallen human cosmos. “His only Son” — the cost of the gift measures the depth of the love; he gave the dearest thing he had. “Whoever believes” — the condition is faith, not merit, not ancestry, not ritual. “Should not perish but have eternal life” — the alternative is real: perishing is the default; eternal life is the gift.

verseByVerse.quote: “God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of the incarnation is salvation, not judgment — and yet judgment is the inevitable corollary of the light's arrival. Those who come to the light are saved; those who refuse are already condemned by their refusal. This is John's doctrine of realized eschatology: the last judgment is not only a future event but a present reality. Those who believe in the Son have already crossed from death to life (5:24); those who reject him remain under wrath (v. 36). The cross does not create the condemnation; it reveals and resolves it. Salvation is not the avoidance of a future threat but the present possession of eternal life in the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Baptist's final testimony closes with the starkest antithesis in the Gospel. Eternal life and the wrath of God are the only two options. Note that “does not obey” is the negative counterpart to “believes” — in John's vocabulary, genuine faith and genuine obedience are inseparable. Belief without obedience is not saving faith. The “wrath of God” that “remains” (menei — the same verb as “abide,” used for the Spirit's permanent presence and the believer's union with Christ) is not an arbitrary divine anger but the settled, holy opposition of a righteous God to all that contradicts his nature. The cross absorbs this wrath for those who believe.

3.theology: Regeneration and the sovereignty of the Spirit. John 3 is the foundational text for the doctrine of regeneration. The new birth is not a human decision or a religious rite; it is the sovereign act of the Spirit who “blows where he wishes.” Reformed theology has always insisted on this priority: regeneration precedes faith, not follows it. The dead cannot choose life; the blind cannot seek the light; the natural person cannot receive the things of the Spirit (1 Cor 2:14). Therefore the Spirit must first give the new birth — opening the eyes, softening the heart, enabling the faith — and the believing person then truly and freely comes to Christ. This is not coercion but the gift of a new nature that desires what it previously refused. John 3:8 is the pneumatological foundation of Calvinist soteriology: the Spirit blows where he wills, and no human philosophy can domesticate him.
3.examples:
Then: Nicodemus came by night — cautious, half-committed, unwilling to be publicly associated with Jesus. He left the same way, apparently. But something was planted. He will speak up for Jesus in 7:50–51 and will bring a hundred pounds of spices for his burial in 19:39 — he comes out of the darkness into the light, step by step, across the course of the Gospel. The new birth often works like this: slowly, over time, the Spirit moves.

Now: John 3:16 is the most quoted verse in Scripture, which means it is also the most domesticated. Recovering its weight requires hearing the context: Nicodemus, a teacher, a leader, a religious man — told that all of it is insufficient without being born from above. The verse is not a comfort to the self-satisfied; it is the astonishing good news to those who know they are perishing. That is its intended audience — and it always finds them.

4.title: Living Water
4.text: <sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” <sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” <sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” <sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, <sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.” <sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.” <sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people, <sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?” <sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”
4.overview:
The conversation at the well in Sychar is the longest recorded dialogue Jesus has with any individual in the Gospels. Every element of the scene is designed to break conventional boundaries: a Jewish man initiates conversation with a Samaritan woman, alone, at midday. She is the wrong ethnicity, the wrong gender, the wrong moral history. And Jesus engages her with the same depth of theological teaching he will give Nicodemus — the learned ruler of Israel who came by night. The contrast is deliberate: the insider gets the Gospel at night, cautiously; the outsider gets it in broad daylight, at a well, in full public view.

The conversation moves through several layers — water, worship, the Messiah — and culminates in the most explicit self-identification Jesus makes in John before the Passion: “I who speak to you am he.” The woman's response is the model of evangelism: she leaves her water jar (the old, insufficient vessel of her natural thirst) and goes to tell the town. The Samaritans come, hear Jesus themselves, and declare him “Saviour of the world” — the most universally inclusive title for Jesus in the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Living water (hydōr zōn) in the first century referred to running water — a spring or stream rather than a cistern. Jesus appropriates the phrase and fills it with eschatological content: the water he gives becomes “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” — not a one-time drink but an interior, inexhaustible source. This is the imagery of Ezekiel 47 (the river flowing from the temple) and Zechariah 14:8 (living waters flowing from Jerusalem), now located not in a geographic place but in a person. The woman has been going to the well every day to draw water that cannot satisfy her deepest thirst. Jesus identifies her deepest thirst — for meaning, for relationship, for forgiveness, for God — and offers to be its permanent satisfaction.

verseByVerse.quote: “You are right in saying, 'I have no husband'; for you have had five husbands.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' knowledge of her relational history is not voyeurism but revelation — the same divine omniscience that will expose Judas (13:11) and Nathanael (1:47–48). He knows her completely, names her reality precisely, and does not use it to condemn her but to identify himself. She responds by immediately redirecting to a theological controversy (v. 20 — where to worship), which is simultaneously a deflection and a genuine question from someone who has just encountered the holiness of God. Jesus does not pursue her personal history further; he has made his point. The knowledge of God is not a threat but an invitation: he who knows all that you ever did is still sitting with you at the well.

verseByVerse.quote: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The dispute between Samaritans (Mount Gerizim) and Jews (Jerusalem) about the correct place of worship is resolved by Jesus not by adjudicating between the two sites but by declaring the obsolescence of both. True worship is determined not by geography but by the Spirit and truth. “Spirit” points to the new birth of chapter 3: worship flows from the regenerate heart animated by the Holy Spirit. “Truth” points to the revelation of God in Jesus himself (14:6 — “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”). Worship in spirit and truth is worship that is genuine (not formalistic), Spirit-enabled (not natural), and Christ-centred (not location-dependent).

verseByVerse.quote: “I who speak to you am he.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Greek is ego eimi — “I am he,” or simply “I AM.” To a Samaritan woman at a well, Jesus makes the most direct messianic claim in John's Gospel thus far. The context is significant: the woman has just said, “I know that Messiah is coming” (v. 25). Jesus does not say “yes, I am he” as a historical claim; he uses the divine name. This is the first of many ego eimi statements in John, and it sets the pattern: the “I AM” of Exodus 3:14, the God who revealed himself to Moses, is the one sitting at the well in Samaria speaking with a woman the world has written off.

verseByVerse.quote: “We know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Samaritans' confession is the theological climax of the chapter. Samaritans — half-Jewish, despised by both Jews and Gentiles, worshipping at the wrong mountain — become the first people in John's Gospel to confess Jesus as Saviour of the world. Not Saviour of Israel, not Saviour of the religious; Saviour of the world. John's universalism is evangelical breadth: the salvation purchased at the cross is offered to all nations, all social categories, all moral histories. The woman who had five husbands is the evangelist who brings her village to the Saviour of the world.

4.theology: The universality of the Gospel. John 4 is the programmatic text for the cross-cultural mission of the church. Jesus crosses ethnic barriers (Jew to Samaritan), gender conventions (man to woman alone), and moral categories (rabbi to multiple-divorcee) without compromising his holiness. He does so not by minimising the differences but by revealing himself as the one who transcends all of them. The Samaritan woman's five husbands are neither excused nor made the subject of prolonged moralising — they are named, acknowledged, and then superseded by the offer of living water. This is the pastoral logic of the gospel: full knowledge of the person, full offer of grace. The Saviour of the world does not come only for the people the world approves of.
4.examples:
Then: The disciples were astonished (v. 27) that Jesus was talking with a woman — not just any woman, but a Samaritan. Their categories were being dismantled. Every expansion of the gospel in Acts will require the same dismantling: Peter and Cornelius, Paul and the Gentiles, Philip and the Ethiopian. The church keeps having to learn what Jesus taught at the well.

Now: The woman's evangelism was simple: “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.” She did not give a theological argument; she gave a testimony. She did not have answers to every question; she had an encounter. And the village came. The most effective evangelism is often still this: “Come and see” — bring people into the presence of the one who already knows them and is already waiting for them at the well.

5.title: The Son Does What the Father Does
5.text: <sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. <sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?” <sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.” <sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath. <sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” <sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. <sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. <sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. <sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice <sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.”
5.overview:
Chapter 5 moves from the gracious miracle at the pool of Bethesda to the most extensive theological discourse in the first half of John's Gospel. The healing of a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years — on the Sabbath, without the man asking, by a word alone — provokes a Sabbath controversy that becomes the occasion for Jesus' most direct claims about his relationship to the Father.

The discourse of verses 19–47 is the heart of John's Christology. Jesus makes five extraordinary claims: he works in perfect concert with the Father (vv. 19–20); he raises the dead and gives life as the Father does (v. 21); the Father has committed all judgment to the Son (v. 22); those who honour or dishonour the Son honour or dishonour the Father (v. 23); and the Son will call all the dead from their tombs at the final resurrection (vv. 28–29). These are not the claims of a prophet or a teacher. They are either the claims of the eternal Son of God or the words of a megalomaniac. John gives his reader no comfortable middle ground.

verseByVerse.quote: “Do you want to be healed?”
verseByVerse.commentary: The question seems unnecessary — the man has been lying there thirty-eight years. But Jesus asks because healing requires the man's engagement, not merely his passivity. The man's answer is evasive (v. 7 — no one will help me into the pool); he seems to have given up on being healed. Jesus bypasses the system entirely: not the pool, not a ritual, not a waiting game — a word. “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.” The command is itself the enabling: the power to obey is given in the calling. This is the logic of regeneration applied to physical healing: the new birth also comes as a sovereign command that enables the very response it requires.

verseByVerse.quote: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sabbath accusation gives Jesus the occasion for his most concentrated statement of Sonship. God does not rest on the Sabbath in the sense of ceasing all activity — creation rests, but God continues to sustain, govern, and give life. Jesus claims the same: he works in concert with the Father's ongoing work, including on the Sabbath. The implication his opponents immediately grasp (v. 18): he is claiming equality with God. This is not a metaphor or a pious exaggeration; it is a claim to share the divine nature and the divine prerogatives. The Jewish authorities respond with murderous intent — because they understand exactly what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: “The Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This saying sounds like limitation but is actually the expression of perfect unity. The Son does not act independently of the Father — not because he lacks the power or authority, but because the eternal relationship of Father and Son involves perfect communion of will and action. What the Father does, the Son does likewise — in the same way, with the same authority, with the same effect. This is the Trinitarian ontology beneath the Christological claim: the Son's equality with the Father is expressed not in independence but in perfect, eternal, loving correspondence.

verseByVerse.quote: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most important sentences in the entire Bible on the assurance of salvation. Three tenses are compressed into one: the hearing and believing is present action; “has eternal life” is present possession; “passed from death to life” is past tense — already accomplished. Eternal life is not a future reward for present behaviour; it is the present possession of everyone who believes. Judgment is not a future threat for the believer; it has already been adjudicated in favour of the one who is in Christ. This is the realized eschatology of John: the last things are already happening in the present, for those who are united to the Son by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: “An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Having spoken of the spiritual resurrection happening now (v. 25 — “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live”), Jesus moves to the bodily resurrection at the end of history. All will be raised — both the righteous and the wicked. This is the clearest statement in John of a general, bodily resurrection followed by judgment. The voice that called the invalid from his mat at Bethesda will call all humanity from their graves. The one who gives eternal life to those who believe is also the one who will judge those who do not. The mercy and the justice are both located in the same person.

5.theology: The equality and unity of Father and Son. John 5:19–30 is the most concentrated Christological discourse in the Gospels. Jesus claims to do what only God does — give life, raise the dead, execute judgment — and grounds these claims in his eternal relationship with the Father. The Nicene Creed draws on this passage: “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, of one being with the Father.” The Son's equality is not a threat to monotheism but its Trinitarian expression: there is one God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Spirit, and the Son's actions in history are the actions of that one God. Every healing in John points to the final resurrection; every act of life-giving points to the one who is the resurrection and the life.
5.examples:
Then: The man healed at Bethesda had been lying by the pool for thirty-eight years — the same number of years Israel wandered in the wilderness (Deut 2:14). He is a figure of Israel's long, helpless waiting. Jesus heals him without ritual, without water, without a waiting period — by a sovereign word. The old system of waiting and hoping is superseded by the presence of the one who gives life.

Now: The assurance of verse 24 — “has passed from death to life” — is the pastoral anchor of Christian life. When doubt assails, when feelings fluctuate, when sin makes the believer fear judgment, the word of the Son stands: whoever hears my word and believes has eternal life. The judgment that should fall on the believer has already fallen on the Son at the cross. The verdict is in; it cannot be overturned.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted. <sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves. <sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you.” <sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst. <sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day. <sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.” <sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, <sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the longest and most demanding chapter in John's Gospel. It begins with the feeding of five thousand (the fourth sign), moves through Jesus walking on water, and then pivots to the Bread of Life Discourse (vv. 22–71) — the most concentrated and controversial teaching in the Gospel. The feeding recalls the manna in the wilderness; Jesus identifies himself as the true bread from heaven that the manna only prefigured. But this bread is not physical provision; it is his flesh, given for the life of the world.

The discourse is relentlessly Christological and increasingly offensive to his hearers. The crowd wants more bread (v. 34); Jesus offers himself. The crowd grumbles (v. 41); Jesus intensifies the claim. Many disciples leave (v. 66) — the first mass departure in the Gospel. The chapter closes with Peter's confession: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” It is faith in the dark, faith without full understanding, faith that clings not to certainty but to the person who alone has what is needed. That is saving faith.

verseByVerse.quote: “You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus diagnoses the crowd's motivation with devastating accuracy. They have witnessed a messianic sign — the feeding recalls Elisha's multiplication of loaves (2 Kgs 4:42–44) and the manna of Exodus — but they missed the point. They want more bread, not the one who provided it. Jesus distinguishes the sign from what it signifies: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life.” This is the perennial spiritual mistake — pursuing the blessings of God while ignoring the God who gives the blessings. Jesus refuses to be a means to the crowd's material ends; he insists on being the end itself.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of the seven “I AM” statements. Jesus identifies himself with the manna — the bread that sustained Israel in the wilderness — and declares himself to be what the manna only pointed to. “Comes to me” and “believes in me” are parallel: in John's Gospel, coming to Jesus and believing in Jesus are the same act. The promise is absolute: never hunger, never thirst. This is the language of Psalm 107:9 (“he satisfies the longing soul”) and Isaiah 55:1–2. The bread from heaven is a person, and eating him — feeding on him by faith — is the only satisfaction for the soul's deepest hunger.

verseByVerse.quote: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is the most explicit statement of effectual grace in John's Gospel. “Can come” — it is a statement of inability, not merely difficulty. The natural person, apart from the Father's drawing, cannot come to Christ. “Draws” (helkō) means to pull with force — the same word used in 21:6 for hauling in a net full of fish. This is not gentle persuasion but sovereign action that overcomes the resistance of the human will. The drawing and the raising on the last day are linked: the Father who draws is the same one who guarantees the final resurrection of all he gives to the Son (v. 39).

verseByVerse.quote: “The bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most scandalous statement in the discourse. “Eating his flesh and drinking his blood” is not primarily Eucharistic language (though the Lord's Supper is its sacramental enactment) — it is the language of radical, personal faith-union with the crucified Christ. To eat his flesh is to feed on the reality of his incarnation and death; to drink his blood is to receive the life poured out at the cross. The offence is deliberate: Jesus will not allow his hearers to have him on their own terms. He must be eaten — ingested, internalized, depended on completely. Those who refuse find the saying “hard” (v. 60). Those who receive it find eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's confession at the end of chapter 6 is the Johannine equivalent of Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16). It is faith in the dark — many disciples have just left (v. 66), the discourse has been hard, Jesus has asked “Do you want to go away as well?” (v. 67). Peter's answer is not triumphant certainty but the confession of a man who has no better option: nowhere else to go, and knowing it. This is the purest form of faith: not faith based on full understanding, not faith based on comfortable circumstances, but faith in a person because there is simply no one else. “You have the words of eternal life” — wherever those words take us, we must follow.

6.theology: Effectual grace and the perseverance of the saints. John 6 contains the strongest concentration of Calvinist soteriology in the Gospels. The Father gives specific people to the Son (v. 37, 39); the Son loses none of them (v. 39); they will all be raised on the last day (v. 40, 44, 54). This is the chain of salvation: divine election (the Father's giving), effectual drawing (v. 44), present possession of eternal life (v. 54), and final resurrection (v. 54). The perseverance of the saints is not based on the strength of the believer's grip on Christ but on the strength of Christ's grip on the believer: “I will raise him up on the last day” — the action is Christ's, not the believer's. Those who truly come to the Son will never be cast out (v. 37).
6.examples:
Then: The crowd that was fed in the wilderness followed Jesus to Capernaum seeking more bread. When he gave them himself instead, most left. They wanted the kingdom's benefits without the King himself. The same choice faces every hearer of the gospel: receive Christ on his own terms, or turn away to find something more manageable.

Now: Peter's question — “To whom shall we go?” — is the right question for every moment of doubt, difficulty, or disillusionment in the Christian life. Not “is the doctrine correct?” but “is there anyone else?” The answer is always the same: he alone has the words of eternal life. The bread of life is not comfortable or easy; he is necessary. And what is necessary for life, when truly seen, becomes the object of desire.

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. <sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'” <sup>39</sup>(He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.) <sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.” <sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?” <sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?” <sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes place at the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkoth) — the great autumn harvest festival when Israel camped in booths and celebrated the wilderness years, the water that God provided, and the anticipated coming of the Spirit at the end of the age. Every day of the feast a priest carried water from the pool of Siloam and poured it on the altar while the people sang Psalm 118. On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” He claims to be the fulfilment of everything the feast anticipated.

The chapter is dominated by division: the crowds are divided about Jesus (vv. 40–43); the religious authorities are divided (Nicodemus speaks up in his defence, v. 50–51); even the temple police are disarmed by him (“No one ever spoke like this man!”). Division (schisma) is the inevitable result of the arrival of light in a dark world: those who love the light come to it; those who love the darkness retreat from it.

verseByVerse.quote: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The setting is the last day of Tabernacles, the climax of the water-pouring ceremony. At the very moment Israel celebrates God's provision of water in the wilderness and prays for the Spirit to be poured out in the last days (Isa 44:3; Joel 2:28), Jesus claims to be the source of that water. “Come to me and drink” — the same universal invitation as Isaiah 55:1, now embodied in a person. The rivers of living water flowing from the believer (v. 38) are the overflow of the Spirit received through faith in Christ. The gift of the Spirit is the immediate consequence and evidence of believing in the glorified Son.

verseByVerse.quote: (He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.)
verseByVerse.commentary: John's parenthetical comment is theologically crucial. The giving of the Spirit awaits the glorification of Jesus — which in John means the cross, resurrection, and ascension together. The Spirit cannot be poured out in his fullness until the redemption is accomplished, the risen Christ is enthroned, and the new covenant age is inaugurated at Pentecost. The Paraclete — the Helper, the Spirit of truth — is the gift of the glorified Son to his people, and his coming is the experiential realization of everything the Tabernacles feast anticipated.

verseByVerse.quote: “This really is the Prophet.” Others said, “This is the Christ.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's divided responses map the range of messianic expectation in first-century Judaism. “The Prophet” refers to the figure of Deuteronomy 18:15 — the prophet like Moses who would come to speak God's definitive word. “The Christ” refers to the Davidic king. Jesus is both — and more than both. The objection about Galilee (v. 41) is based on ignorance of his Bethlehem birth. The theological point stands: no human category is adequate for Jesus. He is the eternal Word, the Son of God, who can only be named adequately from within the Trinitarian life.

verseByVerse.quote: “No one ever spoke like this man!”
verseByVerse.commentary: The temple police sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed, undone by his words. Their testimony is an inadvertent confession: the authority, the clarity, the depth, the love in his teaching were unlike anything they had ever heard. This is the consistent testimony of all who encounter the teaching of Jesus honestly: “the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority” (Matt 7:28–29). The words of Jesus have this effect not merely because they are intellectually brilliant but because they carry the weight of the one who speaks them. When the eternal Word speaks human language, human language is used beyond its natural capacity.

verseByVerse.quote: “Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing?”
verseByVerse.commentary: Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night in chapter 3, now speaks up — cautiously, juridically, without naming his sympathy. It is a small act of courage in a hostile room, and it costs him the scorn of his colleagues (v. 52). He is making his way, slowly, from the dark to the light. His eventual emergence at the burial (19:39) shows that the seed planted at the night conversation has been growing. John traces his journey across the Gospel as a pastoral model: coming to faith is often a slow walk through objection, partial commitment, gradual illumination. The Spirit moves at his own pace in each life.

7.theology: The Holy Spirit as the gift of the glorified Christ. John 7:39 establishes the Trinitarian and redemptive-historical logic of Pentecost. The Spirit is not given independently of the Son's atoning work; he is the gift of the glorified Christ, the experiential realization of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36. Reformed theology has always insisted that the Spirit's work is Christ-centred: he does not draw attention to himself but to the Son (16:14 — “he will glorify me”). The rivers of living water flowing from the believer are not the product of a second blessing or a special experience; they are the ordinary fruit of union with the glorified Christ through faith. Every believer who has received the Spirit has received the fullness of the promise — and the river runs to eternal life.
7.examples:
Then: The Feast of Tabernacles was the most joyful feast in Israel's calendar — eight days of celebration, lights, water, music, the memory of the wilderness and the anticipation of the age to come. Jesus chose this moment to make his most public claim. The timing was not coincidental; the feast was the sign, and he was the substance. Every joy the feast evoked was a pointer to the joy that flows from knowing him.

Now: “No one ever spoke like this man.” The words of Jesus retain their authority across every century and every culture. When the Gospel is preached faithfully, the same astonishment is still possible — not because of the preacher's eloquence but because the words carry the weight of the one who first spoke them. The living water he promised on the last day of Tabernacles is still flowing. The thirsty are still invited to come and drink.

8.title: The Light of the World
8.text: <sup>12</sup>Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. <sup>24</sup>I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins.” <sup>31</sup>So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, <sup>32</sup>and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” <sup>36</sup>So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. <sup>44</sup>You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. <sup>56</sup>Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.” <sup>57</sup>So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” <sup>58</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.” <sup>59</sup>So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the most theologically explosive chapter in John thus far. It opens during the Feast of Tabernacles — when the temple courts were lit with enormous golden menorahs, filling the night sky with light — and Jesus announces: “I am the light of the world.” The second “I AM” statement takes the feast’s imagery and turns it into a self-declaration. He is what the torches anticipated. Every page of the chapter drives toward the climax: “Before Abraham was, I AM” — the unambiguous appropriation of the divine name of Exodus 3:14, spoken in the precincts of the Jerusalem temple. His hearers pick up stones. They know exactly what he means.

Between the second and the seventh “I AM” statements comes a searching discourse on freedom, truth, slavery, and the devil. Jesus diagnoses his opponents’ spiritual condition with surgical precision: they are slaves to sin, children of the devil, unable to hear his word because they have no place in their hearts for the truth. The only liberation is the truth — which is not a set of propositions but a person: “the truth will set you free,” and “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” Freedom in John is not autonomy from God; it is liberation from sin’s tyranny, which comes only through union with the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The second “I AM” statement. The Feast of Tabernacles involved the lighting of four great menorahs in the Court of Women, whose light illuminated all Jerusalem — a reminder of the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Jesus stands in those courts and claims to be the light that the pillars of fire, the Shekinah glory, and the menorahs all pointed to. “The light of life” — a phrase from Psalm 56:13 — means both the light that gives life and the life that is itself light. To follow Jesus is to walk in the light that dispels not only physical but moral, spiritual, and eternal darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: “You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most famous verse in chapter 8 is habitually quoted out of context. “The truth” is not abstract philosophical truth or scientific fact but the revelation of God in Jesus himself (14:6 — “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”). “Will set you free” — free from what? Verse 34 defines it: from sin. The freedom Jesus offers is not political liberation (which his hearers desire) or philosophical enlightenment (which the Hellenistic world desires) but emancipation from the tyranny of sin and the condemnation it brings. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” — free in reality, not merely in status. The freedom is as deep as the slavery was.

verseByVerse.quote: “You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father’s desires.”
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the most severe word Jesus speaks to anyone in John’s Gospel. He is not characterising his opponents as morally worse than others — he is diagnosing their spiritual paternity. To be “of the devil” is to share his fundamental orientation: away from truth, toward murder and deceit. The devil is the father of lies (v. 44) because he introduced the first lie in the garden (Gen 3:4). Those who reject the truth about Jesus align themselves, whether they know it or not, with the one who has been lying from the beginning. This is not ethnic slander; it is spiritual diagnosis. The remedy is available: “if you abide in my word… the truth will set you free.”

verseByVerse.quote: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.”
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus makes an extraordinary claim: Abraham anticipated and rejoiced in the coming of Christ. The precise reference is debated — possibly the birth of Isaac (a type of the promised Son), possibly Abraham’s vision in Genesis 15 — but the theological point is clear: the entire history of Israel was oriented toward the one who now stands before them. Abraham is not Jesus’ ancestor in the ordinary sense; Jesus is the one in whom the Abrahamic covenant finds its fulfilment and its goal. The opponents’ appeal to Abraham as their father is answered by Jesus’ revelation that Abraham was waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: “Before Abraham was, I am.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most audacious claim in the Gospel before the resurrection. The grammar is deliberately jarring: “before Abraham was” (aorist — a completed past event) contrasted with “I am” (present tense, continuous existence). He does not say “I was before Abraham” (which would merely assert pre-existence). He says “I AM” — the divine name of Exodus 3:14, the eternal self-existence of God. His opponents understand perfectly: they reach for stones (v. 59), the penalty for blasphemy. Jesus is not correcting them for misunderstanding; he is escaping them because his hour has not yet come. He has claimed to be Yahweh. Everything else in the Gospel follows from this claim.

8.theology: The divine “I AM” and the nature of Christ’s deity. The “Before Abraham was, I AM” of John 8:58 is the strongest Christological claim in the Synoptic or Johannine tradition. It is not a claim to pre-existence in the sense of existing before birth (as angels do); it is a claim to the eternal, self-existent being that belongs to God alone. The name “I AM” (Heb. YHWH; Greek ego eimi) is the name that cannot be given to a creature — it names the one who simply IS, who derives existence from no source outside himself, who was never not. Jesus claims this name for himself. The response of the Pharisees (picking up stones) is theologically correct; if he is not who he says he is, it is blasphemy. If he is, it is the most important moment in human history.
8.examples:
Then: The chapter opens with the account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11, textually disputed but ancient and consistent with Jesus’ character). Jesus neither condemns nor excuses; he forgives and commands: “Go, and from now on sin no more.” The one who is the light of the world is also the one who does not condemn those who come to him in their darkness. Both truths belong together: the holiness that says “sin no more” and the mercy that says “neither do I condemn you.”

Now: “The truth will set you free” has become a cultural slogan stripped of its content. Universities inscribe it on their gates meaning intellectual liberation; political movements appropriate it for their causes. But in John 8, the freedom is specific: freedom from sin, from the devil’s dominion, from the condemnation that hangs over every human being apart from grace. Only the Son can give this freedom — and he gives it freely to all who abide in his word.

9.title: The Man Born Blind
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. <sup>2</sup>And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” <sup>3</sup>Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. <sup>6</sup>Having said these things, he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud <sup>7</sup>and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” So he went and washed and came back seeing. <sup>17</sup>So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.” <sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” <sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” <sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.” <sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him. <sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the most dramatically structured chapter in John. It tells the story of a man who begins blind and ends worshipping; a story of Pharisees who begin certain they can see and end in declared blindness. The healing of the man born blind — the sixth sign — is simultaneously a physical miracle and a parable of the entire Gospel: Jesus is the light of the world (8:12), and his coming forces a division between those who receive the light and those who refuse it.

John narrates the story in a series of scenes that trace the man’s progressive confession: “The man called Jesus” (v. 11) → “He is a prophet” (v. 17) → “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (v. 33) → “Lord, I believe” (v. 38). Meanwhile the Pharisees move in the opposite direction: initial investigation → division → expulsion of the man → declared blindness (v. 41). The chapter is a masterpiece of literary irony: those who claim to see are blind; the one who was born blind ends by seeing — and by worshipping the Son of God. This is John’s picture of conversion and of the world’s rejection of the light.

verseByVerse.quote: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples’ question assumes a direct link between suffering and personal sin — a common assumption in the ancient world, rooted in a misreading of the covenant curses. Jesus does not endorse the link; he breaks it. This man’s blindness is not punishment; it is the occasion for the display of divine glory. This does not mean all suffering is purposeful in this immediate sense — Jesus is making a specific point about this specific man’s situation. But it does mean that the question “whose sin caused this?” is often the wrong question. The better question is “how might God be glorified in this?” That is the question that opens the way for the light to work.

verseByVerse.quote: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The method is deliberately earthy: mud made with saliva, anointed on the eyes, washed in a specific pool. Jesus does not heal with a word alone (though he could). He uses means — physical, creaturely means — to accomplish a supernatural end. This is the sacramental logic of Christian ministry: the Spirit works through the ordinary (word, water, bread, wine) to accomplish the extraordinary. The pool of Siloam is the pool from which the water was drawn at the Feast of Tabernacles — whose water Jesus claimed to be in chapter 7. The man washes in the waters of the one who is the living water and comes back seeing. He goes in blind and comes back a witness.

verseByVerse.quote: “He is a prophet.” / “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The healed man’s progressive testimony is one of the most moving in the Gospels. He begins with the cautious “he is a prophet” and moves, under sustained interrogation, to the bold declaration: “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” He is reasoning from the sign to the one who performed it — exactly what John intends every reader to do. The Pharisees, by contrast, reason from their theological presuppositions (he broke the Sabbath, therefore he cannot be from God) and are unable to receive the evidence before their eyes. The healed man is the model exegete of signs: he lets the evidence lead him to the person.

verseByVerse.quote: “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of the chapter. After being cast out of the synagogue — losing his community, his religious standing, his social security — the man is found by Jesus. The Shepherd goes after the one who has been expelled. Jesus reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man’s response is immediate: “Lord, I believe,” and he worships him. This is saving faith in its simplest form: the revelation of who Jesus is received with trust and responded to with worship. He does not yet have a complete theology; he has an encounter. The encounter is sufficient. Faith is not the accumulation of doctrinal knowledge; it is the reception of the person of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The closing irony is devastating. The Pharisees ask sarcastically: “Are we also blind?” Jesus answers: if you were blind (i.e., aware of your inability to see), you would have no guilt — the light would come and heal you. But because you say “We see” — because you are confident in your own spiritual perception — your sin remains. Pride in one’s spiritual sight is the surest evidence of spiritual blindness. This is the consistent teaching of Isaiah 6 (quoted in John 12:40) and of Paul (1 Cor 1:18–25): the gospel is foolishness to those who are wise in their own eyes, and revelation to those who know they cannot see. Blessed are those who mourn their blindness; they will be given sight.

9.theology: Light, blindness, and the irresistible grace of revelation. Chapter 9 enacts what Jesus declared in chapter 8: “I am the light of the world.” The man born blind represents humanity in its natural state — not merely morally deficient but structurally unable to perceive the light of the knowledge of God. The healing is a sovereign act: Jesus acts first, the man does not request healing, he simply obeys the command to go and wash. This is the logic of regeneration: the Spirit illumines first, and the illumined person then believes. The Pharisees’ blindness is the equal and opposite case: those who trust their own spiritual perception cannot receive the light, because they are not looking for it. The chapter is the sixth sign — and like all John’s signs, it calls the reader to examine their own sight: do you see? Or are you, like the Pharisees, confident that you can see when you cannot?
9.examples:
Then: The healed man is cast out of the synagogue — the ancient equivalent of excommunication, social death, economic vulnerability. He loses everything when he tells the truth about Jesus. And then Jesus comes to find him. The one who costs everything is also the one who gives everything back — and more. “Lord, I believe” is spoken by a man who has just lost his entire social world, and it is the freest sentence he has ever spoken.

Now: The question “who sinned?” is still the first instinct when suffering arrives. Parents ask it about disabled children; cancer patients ask it about themselves; churches have been known to imply it about those who suffer. Jesus’ answer remains: stop looking for the guilt and start looking for the glory. The works of God are displayed in the broken places. The light shines most visibly in the deepest darkness.

10.title: The Good Shepherd
10.text: <sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. <sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. <sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. <sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me, <sup>15</sup>just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. <sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. <sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. <sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand. <sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.” <sup>38</sup>“even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 continues directly from chapter 9 — Jesus addresses those who cast out the healed man, who are the false shepherds of Israel. The good shepherd discourse is the most pastorally rich passage in John’s Gospel and one of the most beloved in all of Scripture. Against the background of Ezekiel 34 (God’s indictment of Israel’s false shepherds and his promise to come himself as the true Shepherd), Jesus announces: “I am the good shepherd.”

The chapter gives us two of the seven “I AM” statements: “I am the door” (v. 7, 9) and “I am the good shepherd” (v. 11, 14). As the door, he is the only legitimate access to the Father’s flock — salvation comes through him alone, and he gives the sheep freedom (“go in and out and find pasture”). As the good shepherd, he knows his sheep by name, calls them, leads them, and lays down his life for them. The chapter climaxes in the most explicit statement of the eternal security of believers in John: “no one will snatch them out of my hand… no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.” And then: “I and the Father are one” — the clearest statement of divine unity in the Gospel. His opponents again reach for stones.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The third “I AM” statement. In first-century Palestine, a shepherd would lie across the entrance of the sheepfold at night, literally becoming the door — no sheep could enter or leave without passing over him. Jesus takes this image and declares himself the only legitimate access to God’s people and God’s salvation. “He will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture” — salvation in John is not merely rescue from judgment but entry into the abundant life of the flock: community, nourishment, freedom, the presence of the Shepherd. “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (v. 10) is John’s summary of the Gospel. Not bare survival but overflowing life.

verseByVerse.quote: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourth “I AM” statement. The adjective “good” (kalos) means not merely morally good but beautiful, genuine, noble — the shepherd who perfectly embodies what a shepherd should be. The defining characteristic is self-sacrifice: “lays down his life for the sheep.” The Greek is striking — tithenai tēn psychēn, literally “to place down his soul.” This is not accidental death or martyrdom forced upon him; it is a deliberate, chosen act of surrender. Verse 18 makes it explicit: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.” The cross in John is not tragedy; it is the supreme act of the shepherd’s love, freely chosen, on behalf of the sheep who could not save themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: “I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The mutual knowledge of shepherd and sheep is grounded in and modelled on the mutual knowledge of Father and Son. This is one of the most extraordinary analogies in Scripture: the intimacy of the eternal Trinitarian relationship — Father knowing Son, Son knowing Father in perfect, infinite, mutual love — is the pattern for the intimacy between Christ and his people. “Knowing” in this context is not mere intellectual awareness but the covenantal knowledge of love, commitment, and presence. To be known by Jesus is to be known as he knows the Father: completely, unchangeably, with a love that will not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The most complete statement of the eternal security of believers in John. Three verbs, three negatives, two hands. The sheep hear, they know, they follow — and the result is: eternal life given, never perishing, no snatching out of his hand, no snatching out of the Father’s hand. The security rests not on the sheep’s grip on the Shepherd but on the Shepherd’s grip on the sheep — and behind that, on the Father’s grip, which is greater still. This is the Johannine equivalent of Romans 8:38–39: nothing in all creation shall separate us from the love of God in Christ. The security of the believer is as strong as the omnipotent hands of the Father and the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: “I and the Father are one.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The Greek hen (one) is neuter — not “one person” (heis) but “one thing,” one in nature, will, and action. This is not modalism (collapsing Father and Son into one person) but the assertion of essential unity. His opponents understand it as a claim to deity and reach for stones (v. 31) — the third time in John someone has tried to stone him for blasphemy. Jesus does not correct them by saying “I only meant we’re united in purpose”; he defends the claim from Scripture (Ps 82:6) while reaffirming that the Father is in him and he is in the Father (v. 38). “I and the Father are one” is the ontological foundation for every pastoral promise in the chapter: the security of the sheep rests on the unity of the Son with the omnipotent Father.

10.theology: The eternal security of the elect. John 10:27–29 is the strongest New Testament statement of what Reformed theology calls the perseverance of the saints — or more precisely, the preservation of the saints by God.
