Mary has spoken to angels and to the risen Jesus without recognising him — grief has blinded her, and the resurrection has transformed him. Then he speaks her name, and she knows instantly. This is the fulfilment of 10:3: "the sheep hear his voice… he calls his own sheep by name." The Good Shepherd has returned from death, and the first word he speaks is the name of a weeping woman in a garden. The resurrection is not an abstraction or a doctrine; it is a personal encounter with the one who knows your name. Mary's response — "Rabboni!" — is the word of one who has found, or been found by, what she lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace be with you… As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first word of the risen Christ to the gathered disciples is "Peace" — shalom, the wholeness and rightness that the cross has now made possible between God and his people. The commission that follows is the Johannine equivalent of the Great Commission: "as the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." The pattern of the mission is the pattern of the incarnation: sent into the world, not extracted from it; bearing the Father's authority, not one's own. The breathing of the Spirit (v. 22) is John's Pentecost — the risen Christ imparting the Spirit to his disciples, fulfilling the promise of chapters 14–16. The church is born in the locked room by the breath of the risen Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Thomas' confession is the theological summit of the Gospel and the direct answer to its opening verse: "the Word was God" (1:1). Thomas, who demanded empirical proof (v. 25), receives it — and his response goes far beyond what the evidence strictly requires. He does not merely say "you are risen" or "you are the Messiah"; he says "my Lord and my God" — the full divine name, applied personally and possessively. This is the model of Christian confession: not "Jesus is a significant religious figure" but "my Lord and my God." Jesus' response gently corrects the dependency on sight ("because you have seen me you have believed") and pronounces the beatitude that encompasses every subsequent generation: "blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed."

verseByVerse.quote: "These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name."
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose statement of the Gospel. John did not write to record history for its own sake, to provide a biography of Jesus, or to compile a theological treatise. He wrote so that readers would believe — pisteuō, the active, personal trust that receives the person of Christ — and that by believing they would have life, the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The signs were selected (v. 30 — "many other signs Jesus did which are not written in this book") with this purpose in mind: each one is a window into who Jesus is, a rung on the ladder of faith. The Gospel is an extended argument for the faith it invites, and the faith it invites leads to the life it promises.

20.theology: The resurrection as the foundation of faith and the beginning of new creation. John 20 places the resurrection on "the first day of the week" — twice — because it is the first day of the new creation. The old creation began in darkness and chaos (Gen 1:2); the new creation begins with an empty tomb in the pre-dawn darkness. The resurrection of Jesus is not merely his personal resuscitation but the beginning of the renewal of all things — the inauguration of the age to come breaking into the present age. Reformed theology insists that the resurrection is the validation of the atonement (Rom 4:25 — "raised for our justification"), the foundation of Christian hope (1 Cor 15:14 — "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile"), and the pattern of the believer's resurrection (1 Cor 15:20 — "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep"). Thomas' confession is the appropriate response to all of this.
20.examples:
Then: Mary's experience — weeping in the garden, not recognising the risen Lord until he speaks her name — is the experience of every believer who has prayed into what felt like silence, who has stood at a loss in a situation that seemed final. The risen Christ is often not recognised in the form we expect. He comes to Mary as a gardener, to the disciples on the road as a stranger (Luke 24), to Peter by the lake as a figure on the shore. He comes. He speaks our name. Recognition follows.

Now: "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" — this is the beatitude addressed directly to every Christian after the first generation. We have not seen the empty tomb or touched the risen body. We believe on the testimony of those who did, preserved in this Gospel. The beatitude does not call our faith inferior; it calls it blessed. The faith that rests on testimony — on the word of the apostolic witness, on the word of God — is the faith that Jesus himself pronounces blessed. We are the ones he was speaking to.

21.title: Do You Love Me?
21.text: <sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." <sup>6</sup>He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish. <sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. <sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." <sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." <sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep." <sup>19</sup>This he said to show by what kind of death he would glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." <sup>22</sup>"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the epilogue of the Gospel — and it is necessary. The Gospel could have ended at 20:31; the purpose statement is a natural conclusion. But John knows that Peter's story is unfinished. The man who denied three times by a charcoal fire needs a threefold restoration by another charcoal fire — and the risen Lord provides it. Chapter 21 is one of the most pastorally tender passages in all of Scripture: the reinstatement of a failed disciple by the one he failed, on the shore of the lake where they first met, over breakfast that the Lord himself has prepared.

The threefold question — "Do you love me?" — is not interrogation; it is restoration. Each question peels back one layer of the denial, and each answer ("You know that I love you") receives a commission: "Feed my lambs… tend my sheep… feed my sheep." The one who denied the Shepherd is now entrusted with the flock. Love is the qualification for ministry, not performance or achievement. The Gospel ends not with a triumphalist commission but with a personal question: "Do you love me?" Everything — discipleship, ministry, mission, the Christian life — hangs on the answer. The Gospel ends with that question still ringing in the air, addressed now to every reader: Do you love him?

verseByVerse.quote: "I am going fishing." … "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's return to fishing has been read as either apostasy (abandoning the mission) or simply the necessity of eating. Either way, the risen Lord meets him there — not where Peter has chosen to be spiritually but where he is. The miraculous catch of 153 fish (v. 11 — John counts them) mirrors the call at the beginning of the ministry in Luke 5: the same inexplicable abundance, the same recognition of the Lord's identity, the same nets threatening to break. Peter jumped into the water then and left everything; he jumps into the water now and swims to the one he denied. The resurrection has not changed the pattern — the Lord still calls from the shore, still produces abundance, still beckons his disciples toward himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "They saw a charcoal fire… Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast."
verseByVerse.commentary: The detail of the charcoal fire (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament — here and at the high priest's courtyard (18:18) where Peter denied. John is not subtle: the setting of the restoration deliberately echoes the setting of the failure. The risen Lord does not avoid the association; he uses it. He makes breakfast over the same kind of fire that warmed the hands of Peter's denial, and he serves his disciples at the same kind of fire. This is the grace of the resurrection: not erasure of the past but redemption of it, the healing of the wound in the place where the wound was made.

verseByVerse.quote: "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" … "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The threefold question corresponds exactly to the threefold denial. Jesus uses Peter's old name — Simon son of John — not his new name (Peter/Rock), which perhaps gently reminds him of the gap between his calling and his recent performance. The question "do you love me more than these?" (v. 15) may refer to the other disciples (Peter had claimed more loyalty than the rest, 13:37) or to the fishing boats and nets (the old life). Each answer receives a commission: "feed my lambs," "tend my sheep," "feed my sheep." The commission is the restoration: Peter is not benched or demoted but returned to the same charge he was given at Caesarea Philippi. Love is the only qualification. "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you" — when words run out, we appeal to his omniscience. He knows.

verseByVerse.quote: "Follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary: The final command of the Gospel is the first command Jesus ever gave: "Follow me" (1:43). The bracket closes. The Gospel begins with a call to follow and ends with the same call, addressed now to a man who has denied and been restored, who has learned what following costs and what failing costs and what grace costs. "Follow me" after the cross and the resurrection is a richer and more costly command than "follow me" on the shore of Galilee before any of it. Peter will follow — all the way to a cross of his own (v. 18–19 — "when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go"). The love that answers "you know I love you" will be tested and proved in ways Peter cannot yet imagine. "Follow me" is sufficient preparation.

verseByVerse.quote: "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gospel's final word to Peter — and to every disciple tempted to compare their calling to another's — is the most focused command in Scripture: "You follow me." Not "follow me, paying attention to what I am doing with everyone else." Not "follow me, keeping an eye on the beloved disciple's trajectory." Just: you follow me. The comparison with others is the great distraction of the Christian life: their suffering seems less, their calling more glorious, their path more comfortable or more heroic. Jesus cuts through every comparison with this: "what is that to you?" Your calling is not their calling. Your path is not their path. You have been given the command. You follow me. The Gospel ends there — not with triumph or resolution but with a command and an open future. The rest is discipleship.

21.theology: The restoration of the fallen and the nature of Christian ministry. John 21 is the New Testament's most extended treatment of the restoration of a fallen disciple. Peter's reinstatement is not conditional on an explanation, a penance, or a probationary period; it is grounded solely in love — his love for Christ, acknowledged with appropriate humility ("you know that I love you"), and Christ's love for him, expressed in the commission. The structure of verses 15–17 establishes the principle that will govern Reformed pastoral theology: ministry flows from love, not from performance. The question is not "have you recovered sufficiently?" or "have you proved yourself again?" but "do you love me?" The one who loves is equipped to feed. Everything else — gifts, training, experience, temperament — is secondary to this.
21.examples:
Then: Peter's restoration took place at breakfast, over fish, on a familiar shore, in the ordinary texture of life. There was no ceremony, no formal reinstatement service, no public announcement. The risen Lord simply made breakfast, asked three questions, gave three commissions, and said "follow me." Grace often comes in the ordinary — in a meal, in a conversation, in a specific and personal question addressed to the one who failed. The disciples who witnessed this would never forget it. The one who failed most publicly was the one most tenderly restored.

Now: "Do you love me?" is the question with which the Gospel closes — and it remains open, addressed to every reader. John has constructed his entire Gospel to bring the reader to this question: the seven signs, the seven "I AM" statements, the Farewell Discourse, the High Priestly Prayer, the cross, the resurrection — all of it has been building the case for who Jesus is and what he has done. Having made the case, he does not close with a doctrinal summary but with a personal question. Do you love him? The answer determines everything. Peter said "you know that I love you" and received the commission of a lifetime. The same question waits for every reader of this Gospel. Everything hangs on the answer.

22.title: About This Commentary
22.overview:
This commentary on the Gospel of John was prepared as a devotional and theological companion for personal and group study. It follows the same approach as the Isaiah, Ephesians, Acts, Ecclesiastes, and Matthew commentaries in this series: Reformed, evangelical, and doxological — written to glorify God and to help readers encounter the living Christ in the pages of Scripture.

The commentary draws on the Reformed tradition as expressed by theologians and preachers including John Calvin, B.B. Warfield, D.A. Carson, R.C.
